title: It's alive
spec: MCP01 · first boot under the Inspector
intro: Three decorated Python functions, one command, and a browser tab that proves an LLM could call them. Four steps from "I wrote a file" to "a client discovered my tools and got a real result back".

provenance.source: a narrated first run of MCP01's document_server.py under the Inspector; the boot banner, tool names and search result are the module's own, timing and request ids are reconstructed

foot: Run it for real: MCP01 §5 — mcp dev document_server.py, then work the five verification checks.

steps.title: One command, and something is listening
narrative: mcp dev does three things at once: it starts your server as a subprocess, attaches the Inspector to it over stdio, and serves a UI at localhost:5173. You did not write a network layer, a router, or a schema — FastMCP derived all of it from your type hints.

Read the fourth line of the banner before anything else. Tools discovered is the first honest signal that your decorators worked; if a tool is missing here it is missing everywhere, and no amount of prompting will conjure it.

terminal.text:
Starting MCP Inspector...
Connecting to server: python document_server.py

Server connected: document-server v1.0.0
Tools discovered: search_documents, calculate_similarity, save_note
Inspector running at: http://localhost:5173

view.note: No JSON Schema anywhere in the file. FastMCP reads the annotations and the docstring and generates the schema a client will see.

steps.title: The handshake
narrative: Before any tool can be called, client and server agree on two things: which protocol version they are both speaking, and what each side is capable of. That is the initialize exchange, and the Inspector shows it in the Server Info tab.

Capabilities are a contract, not a boast. Your server declares tools because you used @mcp.tool(); it does not declare resources or prompts because you have not written any. A client reads that and never asks for what is not there — which is why an empty Resources tab is correct here, not broken.

view.note: tools and nothing else. Add @mcp.resource(...) later and a resources key appears here on its own — the handshake is generated, not hand-maintained.

steps.title: tools/list — the version of your code an LLM reads
narrative: Click Tools. Three entries, each with a form built from your parameter names and defaults. This is the moment your docstrings stop being documentation and become an interface.

Look at what carried through from the source and what did not. The types came from the annotations, the defaults from the signature, and the description from the first lines of the docstring. Your validation logic — limit must be between 1 and 50 — did not: schemas describe shape, not rules. That constraint still exists, but it exists as a runtime error, which is exactly the distinction step 4 turns on.
steps.youDo: Click Tools in the left panel and confirm all three appear with their descriptions.

terminal.text:
search_documents      Search the document store for documents matching a query string.
calculate_similarity  Calculate cosine similarity between two text strings using word overlap.
save_note             Save a note with a title and content.

data.name: search_documents
data.description: Search the document store for documents matching a query string. Performs case-insensitive substring matching across document IDs and content. Returns a ranked list of matching documents.

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return. Default is 5.

view.note: limit is optional here because it has a default in Python. query is required because it does not. Nothing else decided that.

steps.title: Call it — and then call it wrong
narrative: Enter {"query": "MCP", "limit": 2} and click Run. Two documents come back, ranked: mcp-overview scores 3 because "MCP" appears in both the id and the content, fastmcp-guide scores 1 because it appears in the content only. Your scoring rule, visible from the outside for the first time.

Now do the thing that separates a demo from a server: call it with an empty query. Your ValueError comes back as a JSON-RPC error, and you can read the exact message a model would have to work with. A tool that fails legibly here is one you can debug later; a tool that fails silently inside an LLM session is not.

One caveat before you wire this into Claude Desktop. A green Inspector proves the wire works — it does not predict whether a model will choose the right tool at the right moment. That is decided by the descriptions you just saw in step 3, and the only way to test it is with a model in the loop.

before.title: VERIFICATION — all three tools, both paths

cells: all three tools listed with descriptions

view.text: You now have the smallest complete loop in MCP: a server that declares what it can do, a client that discovers it, and a call that returns real data. Every remaining module in this course adds one thing to this loop — resources and prompts, a transport that other machines can reach, auth, and the defences that stop the data coming back from giving orders. None of them change the shape you just saw.
